title: Exploring Ancient Catalhoyuk
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Catalhoyuk is a very old and large settlement in southern Turkey. It existed from around 7500 BC to 5600 BC. People lived there in mudbrick houses. The houses were built very close together like a maze. There were no streets on the ground. People walked on the roofs.
pages.caption: On-site restoration of a typical interior

evidence.articleCaption: On-site restoration of a typical interior

pages.text: The houses did not have doors on the ground. People went inside through holes in the roof. They used ladders and stairs to climb up and down. Inside, the homes were kept very clean. Cooking was done near the south wall where hearths and ovens stood.
pages.caption: The earliest excavations of the site

evidence.articleCaption: The earliest excavations of the site

pages.text: The people of this ancient town grew crops like wheat and barley. They also gathered fruit and nuts from the hills. Food was stored in special bins. Some statues of female figures were found inside these storage bins to protect the food.
pages.caption: Deep trenches in the site

evidence.articleCaption: Deep trenches in the site

pages.text: Men and women seemed to have equal social status in the community. No big palaces or special houses for kings have been found. Children learned how to build houses and do daily work by watching adults make objects like beads and statues.
pages.caption: Detail of the mural showing the hind part of the aurochs, a deer and hunters

evidence.fileTitle: File:Detail of the mural showing the hind part of the aurochs, a deer and hunters..jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Detail of the mural showing the hind part of the aurochs, a deer and hunters

pages.text: Families buried their dead right beneath the floors of their homes. Archaeologists found many human remains under beds and hearths. Over many years, old houses were rebuilt on top of rubble, which made the settlement grow into a high mound.

Catalhoyuk is a massive Neolithic and Chalcolithic proto-city located in southern Anatolia. Flourishing around 7000 BC, the settlement overlooked the Konya Plain in Turkey. It is celebrated by archaeologists for its exceptional preservation and large size during the early agricultural era.
pages.caption: On-site restoration of a typical interior

evidence.articleCaption: On-site restoration of a typical interior

pages.text: The town consisted entirely of domestic buildings clustered in a honeycomb-like maze. Without traditional streets or footpaths, inhabitants moved across the flat rooftops. People entered their mudbrick homes through ceiling openings using timber ladders and steep stairs.
pages.caption: The earliest excavations of the site

evidence.articleCaption: The earliest excavations of the site

pages.text: Inside, homes featured smooth plastered walls and raised platforms used for domestic tasks and sleeping. Cooking hearths and ovens were typically placed against the south wall. Inhabitants maintained remarkably clean interiors, disposing of rubbish and sewage in external middens.
pages.caption: Deep trenches in the site

evidence.articleCaption: Deep trenches in the site

pages.text: Agricultural activities supported the population, with residents cultivating domesticated wheat, barley, and peas while harvesting wild nuts and fruit. Numerous female figurines have been recovered from the site, with some discovered inside grain storage bins to supposedly protect food supplies.
pages.caption: Detail of the mural showing the hind part of the aurochs, a deer and hunters

evidence.fileTitle: File:Detail of the mural showing the hind part of the aurochs, a deer and hunters..jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Detail of the mural showing the hind part of the aurochs, a deer and hunters

pages.text: Evidence suggests an egalitarian social structure where men and women shared equal status and nutrition. Children learned crafts and rituals by observing adults. Furthermore, inhabitants practiced intramural burial, placing their dead in pits beneath house floors, hearths, and sleeping platforms.

Over centuries, houses were partially demolished and rebuilt on rubble foundations, gradually creating an eighteen-layered mound. Modern archaeological projects have continually uncovered new details about the daily life, mortuary structures, and social organization of this remarkable ancient community.

Catalhoyuk represents a prominent Neolithic and Chalcolithic tell situated on the Konya Plain in southern Anatolia. Flourishing approximately around 7000 BC, this proto-city is globally recognized for its expansive dimensions, remarkable architectural preservation, and indications of an early egalitarian social framework.
pages.caption: On-site restoration of a typical interior

evidence.articleCaption: On-site restoration of a typical interior

pages.text: The settlement was architecturally characterized by an aggregate formation of mudbrick dwellings arranged in a dense, honeycomb-like matrix. Devoid of ground-level streets or footpaths, the community utilized rooftops as thoroughfares, while domestic access was achieved exclusively via ceiling apertures connected to timber ladders.
pages.caption: The earliest excavations of the site

evidence.articleCaption: The earliest excavations of the site

pages.text: Interior spaces consistently displayed meticulously plastered walls, raised platforms for daily activities, and southern-oriented hearths. Scrupulous domestic hygiene was maintained, evidenced by minimal indoor refuse and the systematic accumulation of organic waste and ash in exterior middens.
pages.caption: Deep trenches in the site

evidence.articleCaption: Deep trenches in the site

pages.text: Subsistence strategies relied heavily on cultivated cereal crops, including various wheat species and barley, supplemented by arboriculture and gathered legumes. The frequent recovery of female figurines, occasionally embedded within grain storage infrastructure, points toward ritual practices associated with agricultural protection.
pages.caption: Detail of the mural showing the hind part of the aurochs, a deer and hunters

evidence.fileTitle: File:Detail of the mural showing the hind part of the aurochs, a deer and hunters..jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Detail of the mural showing the hind part of the aurochs, a deer and hunters

pages.text: Sociological investigations indicate minimal hierarchy, with gender parity reflected in comparable nutritional intake and social standing. Spatial organization and genetic studies suggest a community structured around kinship networks, matrilocality, and intermarrying groups inhabiting distinct quarters of the settlement.

Mortuary customs involved intramural inhumation, where deceased individuals were interred beneath domestic floors, beds, and hearths. The continuous cycles of partial building demolition and foundation rebuilding upon accumulated rubble ultimately generated the stratified eighteen-layered stratigraphic sequence observed today.

title: History of the Black Sea Slave Trade
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The Black Sea slave trade moved people from Eastern Europe and the Caucasus to the Mediterranean and the Middle East. This trade lasted from ancient times until the nineteenth century. The Black Sea region was ideal for trading war captives because empires and major trade routes met there.
pages.caption: Mine workers in Greece were often slaves.

evidence.articleCaption: Mine workers in Greece were often slaves.

pages.text: In ancient times, Greek and Roman city ports sold enslaved people. They sent them east to Asia along the Silk Road and west to the Mediterranean world. Ancient Greek colonies traded people from the interior North of the Black Sea. Families sometimes sold their members, or people were captured in wars.
pages.caption: Feodosia and territorial demarcations in the 15th century

evidence.articleCaption: Feodosia and territorial demarcations in the 15th century

pages.text: During the Middle Ages, religious borders created informal slave zones. Christians and Muslims banned enslaving people of their own faith, but they approved of enslaving people with different faiths. The Byzantine Empire imported slaves from the Vikings and from other traders who brought captives to Black Sea ports.
pages.caption: Genoese Castle in Caffa, when Caffa was a major port of the Genoese slave trade.

evidence.articleCaption: Genoese Castle in Caffa, when Caffa was a major port of the Genoese slave trade.

pages.text: In the late Middle Ages, trading colonies from Venice and Genoa took control of the Northern Black Sea coasts. They bought captives and transported them as slaves to Italy, Spain, and the Ottoman Empire. Later, the Crimean Khanate became a major center for the international slave trade.
pages.caption: The battle of Wadi al-Khazandar, 1299, depicting Mongol archers and Mamluk cavalry. During that time many mamluk soldiers originated from the Balkan slave trade and the Black Sea slave trade.

evidence.articleCaption: The battle of Wadi al-Khazandar, 1299, depicting Mongol archers and Mamluk cavalry. During that time many mamluk soldiers originated from the Balkan slave trade and the Black Sea slave trade.

pages.text: The Crimean Khanate made a large income by abducting Eastern Europeans through slave raids. When Russia conquered Crimea in 1783, the Crimean slave trade ended. After that, the Circassian slave trade became independent, trafficking women from the Caucasus to the Muslim world until the twentieth century.

B1-B2.headline: History of the Black Sea Slave Trade

pages.text: The Black Sea slave trade trafficked people from Eastern Europe and the Caucasus to destinations in the Mediterranean and the Middle East. Operating from antiquity until the nineteenth century, this major trade network thrived because the Black Sea was surrounded by shifting imperial borders, conquests, and key routes like the Ancient Silk Road.

evidence.articleCaption: Mine workers in Greece were often slaves.

pages.text: In antiquity, people were sold through ancient Greek and Roman city ports along the Black Sea. Greek colonies engaged in trading captives from northern interior tribes, exporting them west to the Mediterranean or east along the Silk Road. This trade continued even after Greek cities became vassals of the Roman Empire within the Bosporan Kingdom.
pages.caption: Feodosia and territorial demarcations in the 15th century

evidence.articleCaption: Feodosia and territorial demarcations in the 15th century

pages.text: During the Middle Ages, informal slave zones formed along religious borders. While both Christians and Muslims banned enslaving co-religionists, they permitted the enslavement of outsiders. The Byzantine Empire imported slaves transported by Vikings via northern routes, while various traders shipped captives down to Byzantine ports and Constantinople.
pages.caption: Genoese Castle in Caffa, when Caffa was a major port of the Genoese slave trade.

evidence.articleCaption: Genoese Castle in Caffa, when Caffa was a major port of the Genoese slave trade.

pages.text: In the late Middle Ages, Genoese and Venetian trading colonies on the Northern Black Sea coast used unstable political and religious borders to acquire captives. They exported these slaves to Italy, Spain, and the Ottoman Empire. By the early modern period, the Crimean Khanate emerged as another major center of the international slave trade.
pages.caption: The battle of Wadi al-Khazandar, 1299, depicting Mongol archers and Mamluk cavalry. During that time many mamluk soldiers originated from the Balkan slave trade and the Black Sea slave trade.

evidence.articleCaption: The battle of Wadi al-Khazandar, 1299, depicting Mongol archers and Mamluk cavalry. During that time many mamluk soldiers originated from the Balkan slave trade and the Black Sea slave trade.

pages.text: The Crimean Khanate generated massive income by abducting Eastern Europeans through coordinated slave raids. Families of wealthy prisoners could pay a ransom to secure their release, which typically matched or doubled the normal market price. When Russian conquest ended the Crimean trade in 1783, the Circassian slave trade from the Caucasus became an independent route supplying women to the Muslim world until the twentieth century.

C1-C2.headline: Dynamics of the Black Sea Slave Trade

pages.text: Spanning from antiquity through the nineteenth century, the Black Sea slave trade systematically trafficked populations from Eastern Europe and the Caucasus toward markets in the Mediterranean and the Middle East. The geographic configuration of the Black Sea—historically defined by imperial peripheries, military conquests, and converging thoroughfares such as the Ancient Silk Road—rendered it exceptionally well-suited for a commerce centered on war captives.
pages.caption: Mine workers in Greece were often slaves.

evidence.articleCaption: Mine workers in Greece were often slaves.

pages.text: During antiquity, coastal Greek and Roman port cities functioned as conduits for this traffic, dispersing enslaved individuals eastward along the Silk Road and westward into the broader Mediterranean. Greek foundations established along the Black Sea littoral facilitated exchanges between interior northern tribes and external buyers, a dynamic that persisted seamlessly as these municipalities transitioned into Roman vassal states within the Bosporan Kingdom.
pages.caption: Feodosia and territorial demarcations in the 15th century

evidence.articleCaption: Feodosia and territorial demarcations in the 15th century

pages.text: Medieval operations were structured around religious demarcations that prohibited co-religionist enslavement while validating the subjugation of religious outsiders. Byzantine importation mechanisms relied heavily on northern routes utilized by Vikings and intermediary traders, channeling captives through Black Sea ports and Constantinople toward domestic consumption and Middle Eastern markets.
pages.caption: Genoese Castle in Caffa, when Caffa was a major port of the Genoese slave trade.

evidence.articleCaption: Genoese Castle in Caffa, when Caffa was a major port of the Genoese slave trade.

pages.text: The late medieval period witnessed maritime republics such as Venice and Genoa establishing Crimean colonies that exploited volatile political and religious borderlands. These merchant networks redirected enslaved populations toward Southern Europe and the Islamic world. Subsequently, the early modern Crimean Khanate institutionalized large-scale raiding as a primary fiscal pillar, utilizing Caffa as the central hub where captives were processed and transferred to Ottoman merchants.
pages.caption: The battle of Wadi al-Khazandar, 1299, depicting Mongol archers and Mamluk cavalry. During that time many mamluk soldiers originated from the Balkan slave trade and the Black Sea slave trade.

evidence.articleCaption: The battle of Wadi al-Khazandar, 1299, depicting Mongol archers and Mamluk cavalry. During that time many mamluk soldiers originated from the Balkan slave trade and the Black Sea slave trade.

pages.text: While affluent captives could frequently secure liberation through structured ransom payments equivalent to or exceeding standard market valuations, mass subjugation remained economically foundational. Following the definitive termination of Crimean operations via Russian conquest in 1783, the regional paradigm shifted toward the Circassian trade, sustaining a specialized luxury trafficking of women from the Caucasus through Anatolia and Constantinople well into the twentieth century.

title: Hopes and Hurdles in the Korean Peace Process
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Leaders from North Korea, South Korea, and the United States started meetings to bring peace and stop nuclear weapons. Long ago, in 1945, Korea was divided into two parts. A terrible war happened later. A cease fire stopped the fighting in 1953, but no peace treaty was signed.
pages.caption: Kim and Trump in Singapore

evidence.fileTitle: File:Kim and Trump shaking hands at the red carpet during the DPRK–USA Singapore Summit.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Kim and Trump in Singapore

pages.text: In May 2017, Moon Jae-in became the President of South Korea. He wanted to have good relations with North Korea. In early 2018, North Korea sent athletes and a special group of people to the Winter Olympics in South Korea. They marched together in the opening ceremony.
pages.caption: After the Trump-Kim summit, North Korea searched for and returned the remains of U.S. POWs and MIAs from the Korean War.

evidence.articleCaption: After the Trump-Kim summit, North Korea searched for and returned the remains of U.S. POWs and MIAs from the Korean War.

pages.text: On April 27, President Moon met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un at the border. They signed a declaration to work for peace and denuclearization. Later, Kim met United States President Donald Trump in Singapore and signed a joint statement.
pages.caption: North Korea dismantled the various significant parts and permanent structure of the Sohae ICBM missile and satellite launching station.

evidence.fileTitle: File:North Korea Sohae ICBM missile- Satellite Launching Station map.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: North Korea dismantled the various significant parts and permanent structure of the Sohae ICBM missile and satellite launching station.

pages.text: North Korea started to show good signs by dismantling a rocket launch site. They also gave back 55 boxes of human remains of soldiers who died during the Korean War. However, some meetings later broke down, and negotiations faced difficulties between the nations.
pages.caption: A North Korean Unha-3 rocket at a launch pad

evidence.fileTitle: File:North Korean Unha-3 rocket at launch pad.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A North Korean Unha-3 rocket at a launch pad

pages.text: Talks struggled to make progress. A summit in Hanoi ended without an agreement because of disagreements over sanctions. Later, relations grew worse, and North Korea stopped cooperating, leaving the prospects for peace very difficult after a period of hope.

B1-B2.headline: Hopes and Hurdles in the Korean Peace Process

pages.text: The Korean peace process began in an effort to resolve the long-running Korean conflict and denuclearize the peninsula. The division of Korea dates back to 1945 at the end of World War II, followed by the outbreak of the Korean War. Although a 1953 ceasefire ended the active fighting, an official peace treaty was never signed.
pages.caption: Kim and Trump in Singapore

evidence.fileTitle: File:Kim and Trump shaking hands at the red carpet during the DPRK–USA Singapore Summit.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Kim and Trump in Singapore

pages.text: International tensions regarding North Korea's nuclear weapons escalated by 2017. Following his election in May 2017, South Korean President Moon Jae-in sought to improve relations with the North. A diplomatic thaw commenced when North Korea sent a high-level delegation and athletes to the 2018 Winter Olympics, where both nations marched together.
pages.caption: After the Trump-Kim summit, North Korea searched for and returned the remains of U.S. POWs and MIAs from the Korean War.

evidence.articleCaption: After the Trump-Kim summit, North Korea searched for and returned the remains of U.S. POWs and MIAs from the Korean War.

pages.text: Historic summits soon followed. On April 27, Moon and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un met at the border to sign the Panmunjom Declaration, pledging peace and denuclearization. Subsequently, Kim met United States President Donald Trump in Singapore on June 12, marking the first meeting between sitting leaders of both countries.
pages.caption: North Korea dismantled the various significant parts and permanent structure of the Sohae ICBM missile and satellite launching station.

evidence.fileTitle: File:North Korea Sohae ICBM missile- Satellite Launching Station map.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: North Korea dismantled the various significant parts and permanent structure of the Sohae ICBM missile and satellite launching station.

pages.text: As part of initial goodwill gestures, North Korea began dismantling rocket launch facilities and handed over 55 boxes containing the remains of American soldiers who died in the war. Despite these actions, subsequent negotiations between the United States and North Korea encountered severe obstacles and failed to produce a lasting agreement.
pages.caption: A North Korean Unha-3 rocket at a launch pad

evidence.fileTitle: File:North Korean Unha-3 rocket at launch pad.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A North Korean Unha-3 rocket at a launch pad

pages.text: In February 2019, a second summit between Trump and Kim in Hanoi ended abruptly without any agreement due to disagreements over sanctions. Relations subsequently deteriorated, and dialogue stalled as North Korea resumed missile tests and eventually severed communication links, casting doubt on the future of peace efforts.

C1-C2.headline: Korean Peace Process: Diplomatic Breakthroughs and Impasses

pages.text: Initiated to address the protracted Korean conflict and achieve denuclearization, the peace process emerged amid heightened international anxiety over North Korea's nuclear capabilities. The structural division of the peninsula originated at the end of World War II, precipitating the war and the subsequent 1953 armistice, which established a persistent military standoff in the absence of a formal peace treaty.
pages.caption: Kim and Trump in Singapore

evidence.fileTitle: File:Kim and Trump shaking hands at the red carpet during the DPRK–USA Singapore Summit.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Kim and Trump in Singapore

pages.text: The diplomatic trajectory shifted significantly following the May 2017 election of South Korean President Moon Jae-in, who favored renewed engagement. This thaw materialized during the 2018 Winter Olympics, where North and South Korea fielded a united ice hockey team and dispatched an unprecedented high-level delegation, creating momentum for bilateral and multilateral summits.
pages.caption: After the Trump-Kim summit, North Korea searched for and returned the remains of U.S. POWs and MIAs from the Korean War.

evidence.articleCaption: After the Trump-Kim summit, North Korea searched for and returned the remains of U.S. POWs and MIAs from the Korean War.

pages.text: Subsequent high-stakes diplomacy included the April 2018 inter-Korean summit, where leaders signed the Panmunjom Declaration vowing complete denuclearization, and the June 2018 Singapore summit between Donald Trump and Kim Jong Un. These engagements produced commitments concerning security guarantees, repatriating war remains, and partial dismantling of military and launch infrastructure.
pages.caption: North Korea dismantled the various significant parts and permanent structure of the Sohae ICBM missile and satellite launching station.

evidence.fileTitle: File:North Korea Sohae ICBM missile- Satellite Launching Station map.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: North Korea dismantled the various significant parts and permanent structure of the Sohae ICBM missile and satellite launching station.

pages.text: Despite initial optimism, substantive progress toward a comprehensive peace treaty or permanent denuclearization proved elusive. Negotiations foundered due to fundamental discrepancies regarding sanctions relief and security demands, notably culminating in the premature termination of the February 2019 Hanoi summit between Trump and Kim.
pages.caption: A North Korean Unha-3 rocket at a launch pad

evidence.fileTitle: File:North Korean Unha-3 rocket at launch pad.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A North Korean Unha-3 rocket at a launch pad

pages.text: Following the breakdown of high-level diplomacy, bilateral relations steadily deteriorated. North Korea resumed missile tests and adopted a more confrontational posture, ultimately destroying the inter-Korean liaison office in 2020. Consequently, the initial diplomatic openings dissipated, leaving the prospects for a lasting regional peace severely compromised.

The Korean peace process began in an effort to resolve the long-running Korean conflict and denuclearize the peninsula. A1-A2.headline: Climate Change in Middle East and North Africa

pages.text: The Middle East and North Africa region faces big challenges from climate change. The area is very dry and hot. It has low rainfall and dry soil. This makes it one of the most vulnerable places in the world.
pages.caption: Green house gases being emitted from a chimney in a natural gas and oil field in Western Iran

evidence.articleCaption: Green house gases being emitted from a chimney in a natural gas and oil field in Western Iran

pages.text: Greenhouse gas emissions in the region have grown a lot over the past thirty years. Most of these emissions come from the energy sector. Many countries in the region rely heavily on oil and natural gas.
pages.caption: A Sudanese farmer and his land. Drought and low rainfall has severely reduced the farmer's capacity to grow crops.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Kuay Makuach, farmer, Lankien, South Sudan (16902070032).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A Sudanese farmer and his land. Drought and low rainfall has severely reduced the farmer's capacity to grow crops.

pages.text: Climate change causes more droughts, heatwaves, and rising sea levels. High temperatures are expected to get even worse during the summer months. This puts a huge strain on the environment and on people living there.
pages.caption: The coastline of Alexandria, Egypt's 2nd largest city

evidence.articleCaption: The coastline of Alexandria, Egypt's 2nd largest city

pages.text: Water is already very scarce in the region. Most fresh water is used for farming and crops. Changing rain patterns and severe droughts make it even harder to find enough water for everyone.
pages.caption: Mohammed VI of Morocco speaking at the COP22 climate summit held in Marrakech

evidence.articleCaption: Mohammed VI of Morocco speaking at the COP22 climate summit held in Marrakech

pages.text: Many countries are now working to use more renewable energy like solar and wind power. Morocco built a huge solar power station. Nations are also joining international agreements to protect the environment and reduce emissions.

B1-B2.headline: Climate Change Challenges in the MENA Region

pages.text: The Middle East and North Africa region is exceptionally vulnerable to climate change due to its arid and semi-arid environment. Low rainfall, high temperatures, and dry soil create severe climatic challenges. These conditions are projected to worsen throughout the twenty-first century. Without significant emission reductions, parts of the region risk becoming uninhabitable before the year 2100.
pages.caption: Green house gases being emitted from a chimney in a natural gas and oil field in Western Iran

evidence.articleCaption: Green house gases being emitted from a chimney in a natural gas and oil field in Western Iran

pages.text: Human-produced greenhouse gas emissions are the primary driver of these changes. Over the past three decades, the region has more than tripled its emissions. It currently emits above the global average per person. This is largely driven by fossil fuel extraction and reliance on oil and natural gas for electricity generation.
pages.caption: A Sudanese farmer and his land. Drought and low rainfall has severely reduced the farmer's capacity to grow crops.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Kuay Makuach, farmer, Lankien, South Sudan (16902070032).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A Sudanese farmer and his land. Drought and low rainfall has severely reduced the farmer's capacity to grow crops.

pages.text: Climate change is expected to bring frequent heatwaves, severe droughts, and rising sea levels. Summer temperatures are projected to increase significantly. Studies indicate that very hot days have already doubled in number since the 1970s. Rising sea levels also threaten coastal wetlands, which provide essential natural buffers against storms.
pages.caption: The coastline of Alexandria, Egypt's 2nd largest city

evidence.articleCaption: The coastline of Alexandria, Egypt's 2nd largest city

pages.text: Water scarcity is a critical issue across the region, where twelve of the seventeen most water-stressed countries are located. Eighty-five percent of fresh water is used for agricultural irrigation. Shifting rainfall patterns and rising drought frequencies place immense pressure on these already scarce water and agricultural resources.
pages.caption: Mohammed VI of Morocco speaking at the COP22 climate summit held in Marrakech

evidence.articleCaption: Mohammed VI of Morocco speaking at the COP22 climate summit held in Marrakech

pages.text: In response, many countries are establishing national laws and engaging in international accords like the Paris Agreement. Nations are increasingly investing in renewable energy sources such as solar and wind power. For example, Morocco has developed massive concentrated solar power infrastructure to provide clean energy and reduce carbon emissions.

C1-C2.headline: Climate Vulnerability and Mitigation in MENA

pages.text: The Middle East and North Africa region constitutes one of the global hotspots most vulnerable to climate change. Characterized predominantly by arid and semi-arid conditions, the region suffers from low precipitation, elevated temperatures, and depleted soil moisture. According to IPCC projections, these climatic challenges will intensify throughout the twenty-first century, raising the risk that parts of the region could become uninhabitable prior to 2100.
pages.caption: Green house gases being emitted from a chimney in a natural gas and oil field in Western Iran

evidence.articleCaption: Green house gases being emitted from a chimney in a natural gas and oil field in Western Iran

pages.text: Anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions remain the primary driver of these regional vulnerabilities. Over the preceding three decades, emissions have more than tripled, placing per capita output above the global average. This trend is sustained by heavy economic reliance on fossil fuels, with the energy sector generating the vast majority of regional emissions while possessing substantial global oil and natural gas reserves.
pages.caption: A Sudanese farmer and his land. Drought and low rainfall has severely reduced the farmer's capacity to grow crops.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Kuay Makuach, farmer, Lankien, South Sudan (16902070032).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A Sudanese farmer and his land. Drought and low rainfall has severely reduced the farmer's capacity to grow crops.

pages.text: Climatic disruptions manifest as amplified summer heat extremes, protracted droughts, and rising sea levels. Empirical studies demonstrate that the frequency of exceptionally hot days has doubled between the 1970s and 2016. Furthermore, projected sea-level rise threatens to inundate over ninety percent of coastal and freshwater wetlands, degrading vital ecosystem services including storm buffering and carbon sequestration.
pages.caption: The coastline of Alexandria, Egypt's 2nd largest city

evidence.articleCaption: The coastline of Alexandria, Egypt's 2nd largest city

pages.text: Severe water stress characterizes the region, encompassing twelve of the seventeen most water-stressed nations globally. Approximately eighty-five percent of freshwater resources are dedicated to agricultural irrigation. Shifting precipitation patterns, driven by elevated greenhouse gas emissions, exacerbate these deficits, threatening national security and political stability across multiple jurisdictions.
pages.caption: Mohammed VI of Morocco speaking at the COP22 climate summit held in Marrakech

evidence.articleCaption: Mohammed VI of Morocco speaking at the COP22 climate summit held in Marrakech

pages.text: Mitigation and adaptation strategies increasingly focus on renewable energy integration and international policy frameworks. Leveraging high solar and wind potential, countries like Morocco have expanded renewable infrastructure, such as the Ouarzazate Solar Power Station. Concurrently, participation in international treaties like the Paris Agreement and institutional funding plans seek to redirect financial resources toward climate resilience and sustainable development.

title: The Evolution of Climate Activism
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The climate movement is a global group. People work together to ask governments and industries to act on climate change. Citizens and organizations have done activism since the late 1980s and early 1990s. They wanted to influence the United Nations. Activism grew a lot during the 2009 Copenhagen Summit and the Paris Agreement.
pages.caption: Banner "System change, not climate change" at Ende Gelände 2017 in Germany

evidence.fileTitle: File:Ende Gelände November 2017 - Front banner of demonstration.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Banner "System change, not climate change" at Ende Gelände 2017 in Germany

pages.text: Environmental groups take many actions. A big event was the global climate strike in September 2019. Young people joined after Greta Thunberg started Fridays For Future. In 2019, Extinction Rebellion also organized large protests. They blocked roads and asked governments to reduce carbon emissions to zero by 2025.
pages.caption: Climate change march in Washington, D.C. on 29 April 2017

evidence.articleCaption: Climate change march in Washington, D.C. on 29 April 2017

pages.text: In the past, people thought nature could not be changed by humans. Writers started to change this idea. George Perkins Marsh wrote a book in 1864 about human impact. Later, books by Aldo Leopold and Rachel Carson showed how humans harm ecosystems, wildlife, and public health through pollution and pesticides.
pages.caption: Zero Hour Climate March in Pittsburgh

evidence.articleCaption: Zero Hour Climate March in Pittsburgh

pages.text: Activists use different methods to create change. Some use civil disobedience. In 2008, Tim DeChristopher bid on land leases in Utah to protest. Others use legal action. In May 2021, a court in The Hague ordered Royal Dutch Shell to cut its global carbon emissions by 45 percent by 2030.
pages.caption: Students at Tufts University "marched forth on March 4th"

evidence.fileTitle: File:Fossil Fuel Divestment Student Protest at Tufts University.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Students at Tufts University "marched forth on March 4th"

pages.text: Public activism faces many challenges today. Some countries monitor activists closely or place them on watchlists. Activists also face arrests, fines, and new laws against blocking roads. Despite these obstacles, citizen groups continue to demand policies that protect the environment and fight for systematic change.

The climate movement is a worldwide social effort aimed at pressuring governments and industries to address climate change. Since the late 1980s and early 1990s, citizens, environmental groups, and companies have engaged in activism to influence the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. This movement gained significant momentum following the 2009 Copenhagen Summit and the 2016 Paris Agreement.
pages.caption: Banner "System change, not climate change" at Ende Gelände 2017 in Germany

evidence.fileTitle: File:Ende Gelände November 2017 - Front banner of demonstration.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Banner "System change, not climate change" at Ende Gelände 2017 in Germany

pages.text: Organizations use actions like marches and strikes. A major global climate strike occurred in September 2019, organized by groups like Fridays For Future and Earth Strike. Youth involvement grew rapidly after Greta Thunberg began her strikes. Concurrently, Extinction Rebellion organized large protests, blocking roads and demanding zero carbon emissions by 2025 along with a citizens assembly.
pages.caption: Climate change march in Washington, D.C. on 29 April 2017

evidence.articleCaption: Climate change march in Washington, D.C. on 29 April 2017

pages.text: Historically, Western thought viewed nature as unchanging and immune to human influence. Nineteenth-century writers like George Perkins Marsh began challenging this notion. By 1962, Rachel Carson published Silent Spring, exposing how pesticide use harmed wildlife and the food chain. This critique advanced the global environmental movement, while early Earth Day events in 1970 called for broad ecological protection.
pages.caption: Zero Hour Climate March in Pittsburgh

evidence.articleCaption: Zero Hour Climate March in Pittsburgh

pages.text: Activists employ diverse strategies, ranging from civil disobedience to legal challenges. In 2008, an activist disrupted a Utah land lease auction, while others have used hunger strikes and fossil fuel divestment campaigns. In legal actions, courts have intervened; notably, a Dutch court ordered Royal Dutch Shell to reduce its global carbon emissions by 45 percent by 2030.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Fossil Fuel Divestment Student Protest at Tufts University.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Students at Tufts University "marched forth on March 4th"

pages.text: Public activism remains essential for driving systemic environmental change, but it faces notable obstacles. Activists encounter counter-movements, censorship in certain countries, and economic barriers. Furthermore, governments and corporations have sometimes targeted activists through surveillance, legal penalties, arrests, and strategic lawsuits designed to deter public participation.

C1-C2.headline: Dynamics and Strategies of the Climate Movement

pages.text: The climate movement operates as a global social phenomenon focused on compelling state and industrial actors to mitigate the drivers and consequences of climate change. Tracing its origins to efforts surrounding the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change in the late 1980s and early 1990s, the movement expanded significantly in prominence, notably accelerating during the 2009 Copenhagen Summit and the 2016 Paris Agreement.
pages.caption: Banner "System change, not climate change" at Ende Gelände 2017 in Germany

evidence.fileTitle: File:Ende Gelände November 2017 - Front banner of demonstration.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Banner "System change, not climate change" at Ende Gelände 2017 in Germany

pages.text: Tactical repertoires vary widely among environmental organizations, encompassing mass mobilizations such as the September 2019 global climate strikes and disruptive demonstrations by groups like Extinction Rebellion. Youth-led activism, catalyzed by figures such as Greta Thunberg, has profoundly shaped contemporary mobilization, pushing demands that range from aggressive decarbonization targets to the establishment of participatory citizens assemblies.
pages.caption: Climate change march in Washington, D.C. on 29 April 2017

evidence.articleCaption: Climate change march in Washington, D.C. on 29 April 2017

pages.text: Intellectual foundations evolved from the nineteenth-century rejection of human-induced environmental change, as articulated by George Perkins Marsh. Subsequent milestones, including Rachel Carson's critique of indiscriminate pesticide use in Silent Spring and the institutionalization of Earth Day in 1970, expanded public consciousness regarding ecological vulnerability and systemic government failures in environmental protection.
pages.caption: Zero Hour Climate March in Pittsburgh

evidence.articleCaption: Zero Hour Climate March in Pittsburgh

pages.text: Modern climate advocacy integrates a complex spectrum of approaches, categorized by sociologists into transformational strategies such as interstitial, ruptural, and symbiotic actions. Activists utilize civil disobedience, hunger strikes, financial divestment campaigns, and targeted climate litigation. Judicial mechanisms have yielded significant rulings, such as the district court of The Hague mandating substantial carbon reductions from Royal Dutch Shell.

pages.text: Despite its role in fostering reform, public activism confronts substantial structural impediments. These include ideological divergence, counter-movement opposition, and severe political barriers in nations characterized by state surveillance and censorship. Furthermore, activists frequently navigate state and corporate countermeasures, including domestic intelligence watchlists, strategic lawsuits against public participation, and increased legal penalties for infrastructure interference.
